stem: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to progressively worsening shortness of breath that began abruptly 3 hours ago.  He has severe aortic stenosis and is awaiting aortic valve replacement.  Blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg and pulse is 130/min with an irregularly irregular rhythm.  ECG shows new-onset atrial fibrillation with evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy and no significant ST-segment or T-wave changes.  Chest x-ray demonstrates bilateral pulmonary edema.  Which of the following most likely triggered this patient's current presentation?​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​

options.label: A
options.text: Sudden decrease in left ventricular preload

options.label: B
options.text: Sudden decrease in right ventricular contractility

options.label: C
options.text: Sudden increase in left ventricular afterload

options.label: D
options.text: Sudden increase in left ventricular filling

explanation:
This patient's shortness of breath, pulmonary edema, and hypotension are consistent with acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF).  This was likely triggered by the sudden decrease in left ventricular (LV) preload that occurs with atrial fibrillation.  Severe aortic stenosis (AS) predisposes to atrial fibrillation because elevated LV filling pressures are transmitted back to the left atrium, causing left atrial dilation.

Severe AS is considered "preload dependent," meaning that adequate LV preload is needed to maintain forward blood flow.  Reductions in preload are poorly tolerated due to the following effects:

  • LV pressure overload leads to concentric hypertrophy, which reduces LV compliance and makes diastolic filling more difficult.  As a result, the stiff left ventricle relies heavily on atrial contraction to complete filling at the end of diastole.

  • During systole, the LV must generate high pressure to propel blood across the stenotic aortic valve.  Because contractile force increases with end-diastolic volume (Frank-Starling mechanism), adequate diastolic filling helps maintain stroke volume against this elevated afterload.

When atrial fibrillation develops in severe AS, loss of atrial contraction substantially decreases LV filling.  The rapid ventricular rate that often accompanies atrial fibrillation (130/min in this patient) further contributes via decreased diastolic filling time.  With the sudden reduction in LV preload, stroke volume across the stenotic valve decreases, causing hypotension.  At the same time, the left atrium empties incompletely into the stiff left ventricle; although LV end-diastolic volume falls, left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise, causing pulmonary edema.

(Choice B)  A sudden decrease in right ventricular contractility (eg, right ventricular myocardial infarction) can cause right-sided heart failure and hypotension.  However, pulmonary edema is not expected because reduced right ventricular output lowers pulmonary venous pressure.

(Choice C)  A sudden increase in LV afterload (eg, hypertensive emergency) can precipitate ADHF with flash pulmonary edema; however, this patient is hypotensive.

(Choice D)  A sudden increase in LV filling (eg, excessive intravenous fluid administration) can precipitate ADHF in patients with underlying heart failure.  However, this patient's new-onset atrial fibrillation would instead decrease LV filling; his pulmonary edema reflects elevated left atrial pressure from impaired emptying into the stiff left ventricle.

Educational objective:In severe aortic stenosis, the hypertrophied, stiff left ventricle depends on adequate preload, including atrial contraction, to maintain forward blood flow.  Atrial fibrillation abruptly decreases preload through loss of atrial contraction, which can trigger acute decompensated heart failure with hypotension and pulmonary edema.​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​
